item.title: Forget “Malaise 2.0,” GM says it’s still all-in on EVs and autonomy
item.description:
General Motors’ plans will require quite a lot of customers’ trust.

It’s easy to criticize US automakers and their tepid approach to electric vehicles under the current administration and the expiration of theEV tax credit. It’s also easy to look at the rest of the world’s embrace of EVs and wonder if the US is entering a “Malaise 2.0” era. Which is why GM wants the world to know that it is still focused on its end goals of electrification, autonomy, and improving vehicle quality while reducing development time.

At this year’s GM Forward event, company executives announced that its hands-off, eyes-off Super Cruise technology will expand across the lineup and be available on nearly every vehicle. This will include the pickup trucks and the crossovers, and not just the Escalade IQ that it was announced for last year.

Sterling Anderson, GM’s head of product, said the company is testing this technology to the tune of 1 million miles (1.6 million km) a month in both the virtual and real world. The goal is that not only would the vehicle be able to take you places, but it could go and do things for you.

That sounds rather dystopian. But Anderson told Ars in an interview that once you realize what your vehicle is capable of doing (beyond the paradigm of being a car to go places), it opens up a world of convenience that might be hard to envision right now. He’s not talking about an Optimus-style robot that’ll do your laundry, but a tool that you use every day that expands to do more things.

GM’s newly announced OnStar AI will play a role. “Imagine you worked late, and you get in your car to go home,” he told us. “Your car might remember that you ordered takeout from a restaurant recently that you frequent and like. The car could prompt you and place a pick-up order for you, which will be ready when you arrive to pick it up.”

Trust is the key here, and Anderson reiterated that several times, suggesting that a car might be a more trusted piece of technology than a mobile phone. “People have a relationship with their cars that they don’t have with other things,” he said. “If your phone randomly suggested your favorite restaurant, it might give you pause, but if your car did so within the appropriate context you might be more willing to accept that.”

OnStar AI will do more than just learn your habits; it will be able to help you better understand and better use your vehicle, we’re told. For example: a driver hears the car beep but doesn’t know what the alert was for. In this case, they could ask OnStar and it would be able to tell them—for example, a speed limit warning. Being a specialized AI trained specifically on the details of the car, it can be integrated in a way that other models, like Google’s Gemini, cannot.

Thanks to new compute on board, announced at last year’sForward, the car will be able to handle much of that processing locally without requiring a connection to the cloud at all. But a cloud connection could improve the drive or make it safer. For some time now, automakers and suppliers have promised systems that crowdsource data to infer and predict road conditions—if you’re driving through a snowy area, and the cars in front of you have had traction control events, you could receive a warning to be extra careful as you approach.

GM also wants to keep customers within its own ecosystem. Imagine a two-car, two-GM OnStar AI household, and you’re late picking up your child from practice. Here, OnStar AI could look and see your spouse is actually closer, swap roles, and re-direct you to the takeout place to pick up dinner. OK, it’s a very specific use case.

Trust continues to be the key. Anderson knows that must be earned, and trust is difficult to get back if it’s broken.

His approach is to put that customer trust first in what he does. For example, GM’s new infotainment system will have the ability to record from the cameras as a dash cam and store that video. And it can upload that video to GM’s cloud to access anywhere. But it is end-to-end encrypted, meaning that when it hits GM’s servers it’s in a format that GM can’t read. If law enforcement wanted to view the video, GM wouldn’t be able to help because it could not decrypt the video.

That is the type of trust that is absolutely needed when dealing with this type of personal data, because there is a convenience to a lot of this. But the opportunity for that data to be misused is also there—it wasn’ttoo long ago that GM was found to be selling customers’ data, often without their knowledge, to insurance companies.

We’ll want to experience GM’s new attitude in practice, of course, but hearing an automotive executive directly address that concern head-on was refreshing.

This all leads into the fully autonomous functionality that GM is working on. Ars also spoke with Rashed Haq, VP of Autonomous Vehicles at GM, about the current state of the level 4 technology, and more importantly, when it’ll be safe enough for customers to use.

“We look at two key factors, safety and roadcraft,” Haq told me.

Safety obviously includes the vehicle’s occupants, but also the general public. And that requires millions of miles of testing in the real world butalso digitally. Automakers like GM will never be able to prepare for every scenario, but it will combine training data with an open vocabulary to assess what information is there and make a driving decision based on that. Haq also reiterated the company’s expectation that when the car is driven by the computer, the responsibility falls on GM and the computer if something goes wrong due to a malfunction.

The second key here is roadcraft. That means making sure that the vehicle isn’t creating a hazard or problem for other vehicles on the road. You’ve likely seen videos where Waymo vehicles are all crowded on a streetblocking traffic: That’s not something GM wants its cars to do.

Eventually, all of this leads back to the idea of a car working for you for tasks that aren’t just driving places. Your car could go pick up your dry cleaning, or at least drive there and wait while someone comes out and deposits the clothes inside it. You could ride to school with a child, both sitting in the back seat, reclaiming some time together because the car is doing the mundane task of driving.

It’s an interesting idea and will only happen if consumers trust GM and their vehicle enough to do that, something we won’t know until closer to that technology maturing.

GM also announced its Gen-4 EV architecture based on LMR battery technology.As we learned last year, the new lithium manganese-rich battery chemistry promises energy densities close to nickel-manganese-cobalt but without that expensive cobalt, making their cost closer to that of lithium iron phosphate (LFP) chemistry cells.

A 30 percent cheaper battery should help GM offer a wide variety of EVs, hopefully including some affordable models, like the now-limited-run Bolt.

If GM can also deliver affordable autonomy, built on a foundation of trust and safety, it’ll be a unique offering from a US automaker and will put the company in a better position to take on the challenges from global competition.

item.title: Sauron recruits his future Ringwraiths in Rings of Power S3 trailer
item.description:
“I will take my place as the conqueror, a sorcerer, a king.”

Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Powerreturns next month for its third season. Prime Videounveiled a teaserearlier this year at San Diego Comic-Con, but we haven’t heard much about the new season otherwise. We now have the official full trailer, and it’s jam-packed with a rising Sauron, who is intent on conquering Middle-Earth with his army of Orcs—with the fractured opposition of elves, dwarves, and men scrambling to figure out how best to stop him. We also meet the human men who will become the Ringwraiths; the showrunners have dubbed them the Nazgnagol (“Rings-servant”).

(Some spoilers for the first two seasons below.)

Prime Videomade a majorinvestment inThe Rings of Powerwhen it acquired the rights to the source material from the Tolkien estate, even committing to multiple seasons upfront. S3 is set seven years after the events of S2 and opens when the war between the elves and Sauron is at its height. Per the official synopsis:

In season three, Middle-earth is at war. Five years have passed since the fall of Eregion. Sauron’s armies have marched across the whole of the world, conquering all in their path. Only a few isolated pockets stand between the Dark Lord and total victory—Khazad-dǔm, where the Dwarves are now sealed deep within their mountain halls, and the elven realms of Lindon and Rivendell, which are protected by their Three Rings.

But deep in the land of Mordor, in his newly completed tower of Barad-dûr, the Dark Lord toils day and night, obsessed with harnessing a power that will bring the last of his enemies to their knees:One ring to rule them all.Now, all the free peoples of Middle-earth—Dwarves, Elves, Men, and Wizards alike—must find a way to come together, in a race against time to prevent Sauron from achieving his goal of utter domination of all life

We’re also getting some new characters this season, most notably Jamie Campbell Bower as Galadriel’s (Morfydd Clark) long-lost husband, Celeborn. Zubin Varla will play Khamul the Easterling of Rhun; Eddie Marsan will play Thrain, older brother to King Durin IV (Owain Arthur); Andrew Richardson will play Anarion, youngest son of Elendil (Lloyd Owen) and brother to Isildur (Maxim Baldry); and Adam Young will play an Orc named Marnukh, who “might not be what he seems.” Oh, and none other than Simon Pegg will voice the fiery Balrog.

The first four episodes ofThe Rings of PowerS3 premiere on November 11, 2026, on Prime Video. The fifth and sixth episodes will be available on November 18, and the final two episodes will premiere on November 25, 2026.

item.title: Hackers got a four-day head start on epic PHP2Shell vulnerability
item.description:
Hackers were already probing the bug before defenders were told it existed.

Amazon has warned thatvulnerabilities in a programming languagethat underpins much of the Internet, discovered using AI tools, are being “broadly exploited” as governments and companies rush to secure their systems.

The world’s largest cloud computing provider on Wednesday said it had identified an attempt by hackers to exploit the bug four days before the weakness was disclosed to the public.

Amazon added the flaws were “now being broadly exploited in the wild.”

The US National Security Agency and UK authorities earlier on Wednesday warned that the vulnerabilities had left websites around the world critically exposed to hacking, as some governments in Europe were reportedly taking sites offline while they patched the two security flaws.

The vast impact of the bugs, uncovered with the help of OpenAI and Google models after being undetected for more than a decade, highlights the ability of AI to upend cybersecurity.

The release of new models earlier this year from Anthropic and OpenAI with powerful cyber capabilities prompted warnings from politicians and financial regulators and led the US government to temporarily limit their rollout.

The NSA on Wednesday warned all organizations using the programming language known as PHP to immediately update their systems or take them offline.

The developers responsible for maintaining PHP released software updates to patch the vulnerabilities earlier on Wednesday.

“These vulnerabilities often provide a direct path to the server’s file system or database,” the NSA said. “If an immediate update is not feasible, it is recommended that organizations take the system offline until it can be fully mitigated.”

Researchers at two US cybersecurity groups, Calif and Wiz, discovered the vulnerabilities. Alphabet-owned Wiz estimated that the compromised programming language powered about 70 percent of all websites in the world.

“Given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory,” OpenAI said on Wednesday. “To our knowledge, frontier AI found these vulnerabilities before attackers did.”

“It highlights how AI can uncover security flaws with Internet-scale impact, but the same capabilities can also help attackers rapidly develop offensive tools and exploits,” the AI lab added.

OpenAI worked with PHP, Calif, and Wiz to verify the vulnerabilities and develop the patches.

The White House said federal agencies were assessing the potential impacts of the bugs on government systems and critical infrastructure.

PHP’s wide presence on the Internet is largely because WordPress, the most widely used website-building platform, is written primarily in PHP and relies on it to function.

The UK’s National Cyber Security Centre said the vulnerabilities could potentially allow a hacker to take control of a website’s server without needing a password or other login credentials. “The NCSC is encouraging UK organizations to take immediate action,” it said.

item.title: This emulator reimagines Nintendo’s Virtual Boy with a full color display
item.description:
Tile-based color palettes go way beyond the four shades of red on original hardware.

Last year, wereported on Red Viper, a Virtual Boy emulator that added a splash ofSuper Game Boy-style colorto Nintendo’s famously failed red-on-black “portable” 3D headset from the ’90s. Now, a new emulation experiment,VBoy Color, has taken the concept to a higher level, using a tile-based palette system that allows for many more distinct colors in each individual Virtual Boy frame.

Rather than simply replacing the Virtual Boy’s four shades of red with four different colors, VBoy Color’sreadme filesexplain how the emulator’s game-specific Color Packs can assign a distinct four-color palette to each 8×8 tile in a Virtual Boy scene. That means the emulator can differentiate between green pipes, grey platforms, and red brick wall inMario Clash, for instance, even though all those in-game objects share the same overlapping red hues in the original game.

The Game Boy Color-esque results feel like being transported into an alternate history where Nintendo invested in a full-color display rather than cheaper red LEDs for the Virtual Boy hardware. The increased contrast between differently colored elements is particularly welcome in games likeJack Bros.orVertical Force, where the original red-on-red display often makes it hard to differentiate the player-character from busy red background elements.

VBoy Color comes with built-in color packs for 15 different games, which actually represents a significant chunk of the Virtual Boy’s limited official library. Tinkerers can edit those packs manually using built-in video tools to color individual screens, teaching the emulator which colors to assign whenever that same tile is used elsewhere in the game.

Unfortunately, the re-coloring process doesn’t work perfectly in the current beta release. For one, the coloring algorithm seems to occasionally miss individual tiles, leading to some flickering, uncolored squares that stand out distractingly from their surroundings.

For another, this coloring process doesn’t work on games like3-D TetrisorRed Alarmthat eschew tile-based graphics for a more 3D wire frame effect. For these, VBoy Color also offers an option that lets you apply new palettes or color gradients based on the apparent depth of each line, making it easier to discern the 3D effect (especially on a flat monitor).

Even in its early state, VBoy Color features some high-quality emulation (built off of previous emulators like VirtualBoyGo and Beetle VB) and useful features like full stereoscopic support on VR headsets or3D monitors. All in all, it’s nice to haveyetanotheremulatorthat goesbeyond accurate gameplaytoactually improveon the experience delivered by original hardware.

item.title: US-backed vaccine trial on babies canceled after international outcry
item.description:
The decried trial was canceled last week before police seized vaccine doses.

Government officials in Guinea-Bissau have formally rejected a clinical trial that would be run by Danish researchers and funded by the US to look for alleged nonspecific harms from the newborn dose of the hepatitis B vaccine. The vaccine dose is currently recommended globally for all newborns and has been used safely and effectively for decades.

In an email to Ars Technica, one of the trial’s lead researchers, Christine Stabell Benn of Bandim Health Project and the University of Southern Denmark, said that Guinea-Bissau’s Council of Ministers “formally reaffirmed its non-acceptance of the study on 16 October.”

The revelation that the study was formally rejected last week comes after news on Monday that judicial police in Guinea-Bissauraided Bandim Health’s offices and seized vaccines. Stabell Benn highlighted that the police search came after the trial was rejected.

Of the trial’s rejection, Stabell Benn wrote: “We regret the decision because we considered the study scientifically and ethically justified, but we respect the government’s authority to decide whether research may proceed in the country.”

The World Health Organization and many outside experts have sharply disagreed with Stabell Benn and her colleagues on the trial’s justifications and design. It has been widely decried as “unethical” because it would withhold the newborn dose of hepatitis B vaccine from half of the participants.

With the country’s high rates of chronic hepatitis B infections, this would put thousands of babies at risk of developing a lifelong infection that can lead to liver cirrhosis, cancer, and premature death. Experts have further said that there is no scientific justification for the study, given the vaccine’s long use and strong safety record.The WHO wrote in Februarythat the trial “posits hypothetical safety outcomes without sufficient credible evidence” to justify putting newborns at risk.

Outrage erupted over the trial after the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention announced in December that it had awarded an unsolicited grant of $1.6 million to Bandim Health, which Stabell Benn runs with her husband Peter Aaby. The researchers are known for pursuing studies on nonspecific harms from vaccines and have been lauded by anti-vaccine advocates, including US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy. But Aaby and Stabell Benn’s scientific peers have been critical of the quality of their work; the researchers are currently under investigation by Danish authorities for alleged scientific misconduct in their previous studies.

Their hepatitis B vaccine trial was reportedly halted in January by Guinea-Bissau authorities. But outcry erupted again after a report that the US CDC, under Kennedy, had onceset another $1.6 million aside to fund the trialand intended to move forward with it.

Stabell Benn and colleagues havepublicly lamented their tie to Kennedy. They have also consistently argued that their hepatitis B study is not unethical because Guinea-Bissau does not currently offer routine hepatitis B vaccine doses to newborns. Therefore, newborns not given the vaccine in the trial wouldn’t have received it outside the trial anyway. The country—which experienced a coup in November 2025—plans to introduce a birth dose in 2028, but it lacks the resources and infrastructure to do so now.

Outside experts, including the WHO, point to ethical guidelines, such as the Declaration of Helsinki, which require trials to provide the “best proven intervention” to participants, regardless of the current standard in the location where the trial is conducted. For hepatitis B prevention, the best proven prevention would be the newborn dose of the vaccine, which is globally recommended to be given within the first 24 hours of life. As the WHO wrote explicitly: “Resource constraints cannot be used to justify withholding proven care in a research study involving people.”

Stabell Benn and colleagues appear impervious to this point. Ina LinkedIn post Wednesday, Frederik Schaltz-Buchholzer, a Bandim Health researcher involved in the trial, blamed the backlash on the “Anglophone media” that “framed [the trial] as dangerous because there would be a control group that would have followed the current vaccine schedule” in Guinea-Bissau.

Schaltz-Buchholzer’s post went on to claim that the media controversy has led to distrust of the hepatitis B vaccine in Guinea-Bissau and fears that the vaccine would pose a danger to newborns vaccinated in the trial, which he referred to as the intervention group, writing:

In the Bissau-Guinean context, it was widely understood that this trial was dangerous for the intervention group. For instance, rumours spread on social media with an omnipresent desconfiança (mistrust) that this was actually a novel vaccine to be tested by the Americans. Based on the Anglophone media coverage framing the trial as dangerous, Bissau-Guinean influencers speculated that the reason to test the hepatitis B vaccine in Guinea-Bissau was that the vaccine is dangerous, and that Bissau-Guinean newborns are disposable.

In her email to Ars Technica, Stabell Benn declined to say what reasons Guinea-Bissau officials gave for why the trial was rejected or why their office was searched and vaccine doses were seized. Ars Technica could not immediately reach Guinea-Bissau officials for comment.

But local distrust of the researchers could have played a role in the rejection and police operation. Stabell Benn said police were directed to investigate the vaccine doses directly, saying:

In its communiqué, the Council of Ministers instructed the competent authorities to investigate the origin, acquisition, transport, storage and traceability of vaccines intended for the proposed study. The Judicial Police subsequently searched the Bandim Health Project premises on 19 October and sealed the fridge containing a batch of hepatitis B vaccines. The vaccines were intended for the proposed study. The study had not begun, and none of the vaccines had been administered. We cooperated with the authorities.

Stabell Benn said the trial will not proceed and that Bandim has no plans to move it to a different location. “The underlying scientific question remains important,” she said. “But any future proposal would have to arise from an appropriate local context and partnership and undergo all required scientific, ethical, and governmental reviews.”

item.title: Meta shocked by $25B fine after N.M. refused to join multistate settlement
item.description:
Meta will appeal a ruling imposing the largest fine Mark Zuckerberg has ever seen.

Meta must pay $25 billion to New Mexico after a jury found the tech giant guilty of nearly 44 million violations of state consumer protection laws.

The largest fine to ever hit Meta came after New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez declined to join an$18 billion settlement Meta reached earlier this yearwith attorneys general in nearly all states.

In hisopinionWednesday, US district court judge Francis J. Mathew said there was no “bright line rule” for determining the appropriate penalty for Meta’s repeated and willful deception of users since 2010 about their “control of data, third-party data misuse, misinformation, hate speech, and equal enforcement.”

New Mexico had asked the court to impose even higher fines, up to $40 billion. The entire state of 2 million people were harmed by Meta’s conduct, Torrez argued, and it seemed dubious that Meta would make meaningful changes unless the penalty impacted Meta’s stock price.

Mathew found that the trial record—which showed that top leadership, including Mark Zuckerberg, were aware that the company, then known as Facebook, was making misleading public representations—supported “the highest level of penalty allowed by the NW Unfair Practices Act.”

“The jury was unequivocal: Facebook systematically misled the public” and “took advantage of the public’s lack of knowledge respecting Facebook’s practices to a grossly unfair degree,” Mathew wrote.

To Mathew, it seemed that Meta made a choice to avoid transparency with users in a bid to capitalize on data they didn’t realize they were sharing and better compete with one of its main rivals, the platform then known as Twitter.

“The violations the jury found were not the product of a single misleading statement or isolated incident,” Mathew noted. “They arose from repeated public representations over more than 11 years, concerning multiple core aspects of Facebook’s platform and business.”

Meta had hoped that New Mexico’s penalty would be more in line with a$5 billion settlementthe company made with the Federal Trade Commission to address the Cambridge Analytica fallout. At most, they expected to pay $3.4 billion, while arguing that anything more would be “unconstitutional,” AP Newsreported.

But Mathew said that the FTC settlement “cannot be viewed in a vacuum” while noting that so far, “penalties, consent agreements, and decrees have not deterred Meta from using deceptive trade practices” since the Cambridge Analytica scandal was first exposed.

“To induce users to provide their personal information to Facebook, Facebook made many false promises respecting the security and control of that data over the course of more than a decade,” Mathew wrote.

In apress release, Torrez celebrated the ruling, calling it “a historic day for New Mexico and for consumers across the country.”

“For too long, powerful technology companies have operated as though their size and influence put them beyond the reach of the law,” Torrez said. “A New Mexico jury found nearly 44 million violations of our consumer protection statute, and this penalty order demonstrates that those violations carry real consequences. We took on one of the largest companies in the world because New Mexicans deserve honesty, accountability, and the protection of their personal information. Today’s result makes clear that no corporation is too powerful to be held accountable.”

A Meta spokesperson confirmed to Ars that the company plans to appeal. Legal experts told Reuters the company has a decent chance at slashing the fine on appeal based on constitutional claims. On top of likely claiming that the penalty is unconstitutional, Meta also feels that “this ruling, and the Attorney General’s approach to enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico,” the spokesperson said.

The eye-popping fine following the multistate settlement appears to be making the company uncomfortable, despite critics claims that New Mexico’s penalty is just a “drop in the bucket” for a company that makes $200 billion annually. On Thursday, the VergehighlightedMeta’s third-quarter earningsreport, which showed the company paid close to $10 billion for the multistate settlement. Without that expense, Meta’s income from operations would have been $22 billion higher, the report said.

The excessive penalties come asMeta attempts to reboot its struggling AI strategy, and Meta appeared to signal to Donald Trump’s administration to possibly support its appeal by nodding to its AI wing in its statement opposing the ruling.

“At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online,” Meta’s spokesperson said. “We are confident we will prevail on appeal. In the meantime, Meta will continue to build a safe and free platform to connect millions of Americans, grow small businesses, and help the country maintain its competitive edge.”

Nidhi Hegde, executive director of a watchdog nonprofit called the American Economic Liberties Project, told AP News that Meta users want more enforcers willing to take the company to trial rather than settle matters in ways that the FTC settlement suggested weren’t genuine.

In his opinion, Mathew noted that the jury found that Meta internal messages and investigation results showed that “rather than seek to educate Facebook’s users… Zuckerberg chose instead to capitalize on that lack of understanding in order to manipulate users into sharing more of their personal information publicly.” In one message, Zuckerberg was found laying out a plan to deceive users, saying, “Give them a chance to change their privacy settings but obviously don’t encourage it.”

The company also failed to notify users when apps misused their data, only flagging two of 2,000 unique apps associated with data misuse, Mathew said. Following its investigation, Meta’s “decision was deliberately made to narrow Facebook’s internal definition of data misuse so that Facebook would not have to notify as many people due to the operational burden of doing so,” he wrote.

Additionally, Facebook continued knowingly profiting off of pages with misinformation and hate speech, Mathew wrote. Internal research found “substantial amounts of misleading, false, and possibly false political, health, and science content,” with Meta documenting a “greater concentration of false content in top performing advertising content than in top performing Facebook content.”

Rather than share that research, Meta buried it, while also deceiving users in dozens of other ways, including by misrepresenting that the average Facebook users gets “equal treatment” to celebrities and influencers. While Meta claimed everyone was treated the same, one class of users received warning to remove violating content before strikes were applied and frequently got harmful or sketchy content decisions overturned in cases where most users would not.

Hegde told AP News that she thinks as Meta and other company’s AI products grow more popular, it will be increasingly important for states to remain watchful and protect residents from unknown harms.

“Right now, they are rolling out Muse, an AI assistant encouraging people to trust it with everything from their bank accounts to their medical information,” Hegde said. “Which is why we need more enforcers with courage and laws with actual teeth to rein them in.”

Torrez vowed to keep watch in New Mexico and to continue using the blueprint from the Meta case to enforce consumer protection laws and prevent tech giants’ misuse of data.

“This case has always been about more than one company or one scandal,”Torrez said. “It is about whether corporations can mislead consumers about what happens to their personal information without facing meaningful consequences. New Mexico stood its ground, took this case to trial, and secured a verdict establishing millions of violations of our law. This outcome reinforces a fundamental principle, companies that do business in our state must follow our laws and respect the rights of our people.”

]]>

item.title: US official: Russia’s stalker satellite sure looks like an orbital weapon
item.description:
The Russian official who called commercial satellites “legitimate targets” now says concerns are “unfounded.”

Four years ago, a senior official in Russia’s foreign ministry painted a bullseye on commercial satellite networks that assist Ukraine in its fight against invading Russian military forces.

On Wednesday, several days after a Russian military spacecraft moved within striking distance of one of those commercial satellites, the same Russian diplomat assured the world there’s no reason to worry.

There’s a sharp incongruity in those statements fromKonstantin Vorontsov, deputy head of Russia’s delegation to the United Nations.Vorontsov’s comments Wednesday in the UN General Assembly’s First Committee came moments after a US official called attention torecent maneuvers by Kosmos 2612, a Russian military craft that approached a US-registered commercial satellite some 340 miles (550 kilometers) above Earth.

“Just last weekend, Russia’s Ministry of Defense Kosmos 2612 exhibited threatening behavior by intentionally maneuvering dangerously close to a commercial satellite,” Brian Hardesty, a US State Department official, told the UN committee. “These behaviors appear consistent with an on-orbit weapons operation. The decision to conduct these activities was deliberately reckless and violated long-established safety thresholds in low-Earth orbit.”

Thomas DiNanno, the US Under Secretary of State for Arms Control and International Security, shared a similarstatement on X. The comments were the first from the US government since the close encounter last weekend.

Vorontsov said the US government’s concerns, echoed by European officials, were “unfounded” distractions. “Western countries headed by the United States continue to use loudspeaker diplomacy repeating absurd accusations about Russia’s space activity.”

All Russian activity in space is “purely peaceful in character,” Vorontsov said. “This applies to the activity related to Kosmos 2612.”

Vorontsov’s statements in 2022 were more provocative. At that time, as Ukraine ramped up its reliance on commercial satellite communications and surveillance, Vorontsov said that commercial space infrastructure used by Ukraine’s military, including Western satellites, could be a “legitimate target for a retaliatory strike.”

It is no wonder, then, that the Russian military’s unprecedented maneuvers near one of those satellites raised alarms. Since its launch in April, Kosmos 2612 performed a series of carefully choreographed rocket burns to match orbits with ICEYE-X36, a radar surveillance satellite owned by the US subsidiary of the Finnish remote sensing company ICEYE.

These maneuvers followseveral Russian testsin recent years of suspected anti-satellite (ASAT) weapons, including a system called Nivelir, which can fire a projectile at high speed to smash into another object in orbit. Russia’s co-orbital ASAT experiments date back to the Soviet era.

“Countries can, of course, deny until they are blue in the face that they have weapons in orbit, but observable and confirmable behaviors are hard to deny,” said Jessup Taylor, the US Deputy Permanent Representative to the Conference on Disarmament. “What you do up there speaks much louder than what you say down here.”

Last week, Kosmos 2612 moved closer and held position in “extreme proximity” to ICEYE-X36, according to orbital intelligence company LeoLabs. An executive at LeoLabs told Ars on Monday that Kosmos 2612 moved within 500 meters (about 1,640 feet) of the ICEYE satellite, and likely much closer. An image from Vantor, a satellite remote-sensing company,first published by Axios, showed the satellites about 1 kilometer apart on Saturday.

Taylor suggested Wednesday that Kosmos 2612 may have ultimately closed within a range of 100 feet. It’s hard to know for sure due to the limitations of satellite tracking.

“I would note that Russia did not attempt to explain why a Russian military satellite moved within tens of meters of another country’s commercial satellite,” Taylor said. “The decision to conduct operations violated long-established safety thresholds in low-Earth orbit.”

Kosmos 2612 backed off from ICEYE-X36 without firing a shot and is orbiting far away, although its trajectory does not preclude attempting another approach.

In September, Pentagon officials acknowledged for the first time that the US military possesses space-based weapons. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink announced the news, but he did not reveal any information about the weapons. The United States, Russia, China, and India previously tested ground-launched anti-satellite missiles, but the US government is the first to admit the placement of weapons in orbit.

Examples of China’s weapons testing in space include a 2021 demonstration of aFractional Orbital Bombardment System, and demos of robotic arms and highly maneuverable satellites that could be used for servicing and repair or the inspection and capture of an adversary’s spacecraft.

Much of the discussion at the UN on Wednesday focused on proposals by Russia and China for an international agreement to ban the placement of any weapons in space. US officials say such proposals are moot because the world’s leading space powers already possess them. There’s also the thorny question of how to determine what constitutes a weapon in space, where ramming and jamming could be done by conventional technologies flying on many kinds of satellites.

Such blanket bans are “ineffectual and unrealistic,” Hardesty said. They would “inevitably be violated by its proponents while interfering with our ability to defend against those who would cheat on their obligations.”

Instead, US officials have underscored a tenet of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which bans weapons of mass destruction in orbit. In 2024, under the Biden administration, the United States proposed a resolution in the UN Security Council that would have reaffirmed the ban, two months after a US intelligence leak suggested Russia was developing a nuclear-armed anti-satellite weapon. Russiavetoed the UN resolution.

All of this is happening amid a slowdown in SpaceX’s Starlink or Starshield broadband service in Ukraine, affecting the country’s use of satellite connectivity to support drone operations. The decision to restrict Starlink service in Ukraine,whether directed by SpaceX or the US government, came after President Trump and Elon Musk criticized Ukraine for attacking Russian diesel refineries.

Satellites like the ICEYE platform, meanwhile, provide overhead imaging to support Ukraine’s efforts to target Russian battlefield forces and strike deeper into Russian territory.

item.title: Samsung all but confirms iPhone Duo is goosing Galaxy Z8 sales
item.description:
Searches for Samsung foldables just happened to skyrocket following iPhone Duo unveiling.

Android-powered foldable phones have been available for years, but most people never paid attention to them. As predicted, that could be changing now that Apple has entered the folding phone market with theiPhone Duo. Analysts have speculated thatSamsung’s Z8 foldableswere seeing a boost from the iPhone announcement, and now Samsung has seemingly confirmed that.

In a newblog post, Samsung UK crows that the company’s 2026 foldable lineup is moving much faster than last year’s models. Compared to the Galaxy Z Fold 7, combined European sales for the Galaxy Z Fold 8 andGalaxy Z Fold 8 Ultraare up 45 percent. Samsung isn’t talking about Z Flip 8 sales, but it previously noted that its larger foldables made up about 80 percent of foldable purchases. We can assume any increase there is not impressive enough to mention.

The reason for flat Z Flip sales may simply be that Apple didn’t release a flip phone. Unsurprisingly, Samsung doesn’t mention Apple or the iPhone Duo in its press release. However, it does say that search volume for the Z8 series across Europe spiked 460 percent the week of September 6 to 12. And guess what was announced on September 9? Yep, the iPhone Duo. Z Fold 8 search volume across the entire month of September (when the phones launched) was up 260 percent.

Samsung noted last month that US preorders for the Galaxy Z8 series were trending 30 percent higher than last year, but it hasn’t confirmed any updated numbers for the US market. This meshes with third-party reports, which claimed Samsung was ramping up foldable manufacturing, particularly of the wider, iPhone-like Z Fold 8. The company isn’t talking about the proportion of Z Fold 8 versus Z Fold 8 Ultra sales, but it seems likely that Samsung’s wider foldable is doing better in the wake of Apple’s foldable announcement.

Samsung released its first foldable phone in 2019, and it was the only company seriously pursuing the form factor for several years. Those early devices were clunky and more interesting as feats of engineering than as things you’d want to carry around all day, but little by little, foldable hardware improved until Apple could finally release the product it wanted. The iPhone Duo is not an island—it relies on many of the same components as other foldable phones, including Samsung displays.

The Apple hype train is unstoppable, so increased interest in foldables was probably inevitable. Samsung expanded its foldable lineup with the non-Ultra model just in time, likely based on leaks of Apple’s device. But the wider form factor isn’t just a gimmick—it addresses several annoying issues with foldable phones. The main display is better for watching video with less wasted space. It’s also better for reading documents and using unoptimized apps (many of which are in the Play Store) in portrait orientation compared to square foldable screens. This is a positive change for foldable phones, and one we’ll probably see replicated by other OEMs in the coming months.

Regardless, foldable pricing is definitelynotcool. It’s hard to justify spending $2,000 on a phone, but at the same time, all devices are getting more expensive. With recent price hikes, the top-end flat phones from Samsung, Google, and Apple are only a few hundred dollars away from their foldable options. Foldable prices have inched upward, too, but not by the same amount. Apple even managed an uncharacteristically competitive (for a foldable) price of $2,000 for the iPhone Duo. Samsung’s wide foldable is a little cheaper at $1,900, and it has been discounted at a few retailers since launch.

item.title: Electric or gas? BMW goes both ways with new 2027 X5 and iX5.
item.description:
460 kW charging and 450 miles of range are among the reasons the EV is the one to get.

When we first drove BMW’s first Neue Klasse model,the iX3, it quickly revealed that BMW knows how to make a good electric vehicle. A clean-sheet design, it featured the automaker’ssixth-generation electric powertrain, a completely reimagined dashboard, and powerful computers to run the whole show. Now, much of that technology is being ported over to the larger X5 line.

But BMW knows not all its customers are ready to go electric, especially in the US, so it’s sticking with its powertrain-agnostic CLAR platform, as used in cars as diverse as the large 7 Series and the new gasoline 3 Series. Which means in addition to the all-electric iX5, there are also mild hybrid and plug-in hybrid X5s available, and in time, even a hydrogen-powered option. For now, as I’ll explain, I think the EV is the pick of the bunch.

The most conventional option is the X5 40 xDrive, powered by a 3.0 L turbocharged inline six-cylinder engine that generates 394 hp (294 kW) and 428 lb-ft (580 Nm). The 48 V mild hybrid system can contribute a decent slug of torque (148 lb-ft/200 Nm) if necessary, and the engine operates under the Miller cycle for better efficiency, as well as featuring the usual BMW engine technology, like variable valve timing. Expect around 26 mpg (9 L/100 km) from this powertrain and a full-to-empty range of 569 miles (915 km).

In time, a 400 V plug-in hybrid X5 50e xDrive will join the mix on the production line at Spartanburg, South Carolina, with a 26.5 kWh battery pack and about 44 miles (71 km) of electric range. And eventually, BMW’s hydrogen fuel cell tech will find its way under the hood of the new-generation X5 too. But those wanting something more efficient than the X5 40 can consider the iX5.

BMW is sticking with its strategy of an asynchronous motor for the front axle and an electrically excited synchronous motor for the rear drive unit, thanks to the lower losses of these motor types compared to motors that use permanent magnets. There is a combined output of 570 hp (425 kW) and 593 lb-ft (804 Nm): The front motor generates 245 hp (183 kW) and 225 lb-ft (305 Nm); the rear produces up to 325 hp (242 kW) and 369 lb-ft (500 Nm).

Between the axles at the heart of the iX5 is a rather massive 144 kWh (usable) battery pack, made up of BMW’s new 120 mm cylindrical cells. These are taller than the 95 mm cells in the iX3, which increases energy density by 30 percent over the smaller SUV’s pack. So even if it’s not quite as long-legged as the gas X5, it should still get 450 miles (724 km) on the EPA test cycle, BMW told us. The car’s route planning is designed to take charging into account and uses onboard AI to “consider expected charging capacity, reliability, and precise station location data when selecting stops.” It will even automatically open the charging port flap when you arrive.

Like the smaller Neue Klasse EVs, the pack operates at 800 V, but it is even more capable when it comes to DC fast charging. At a demo during the first drive in California, we watched as an iX5 plugged in at 10 percent state of charge. Within a little over nine minutes, the EV had reached 50 percent SoC, peaking at 465 kW and averaging 375 kW throughout the session, which delivered 61.5 kWh. (The IONNA station had been specially upgraded to charge above the usual 400 kW.) While that kind of power level is now old hat for some Chinese automakers, it’s a big step forward for a European OEM.

A 10–80 percent fast charge takes as little as 22 minutes—provided you have access to a 460 kW charger—via the NACS port. That same port will accept up to 15.4 kW of AC power via BMW’s home charger, or you can use the provided 11 kW onboard AC charger. There are adapters for both V2H and V2L, as the X5 is capable of bidirectional charging.

For decades, BMW’s orange-lit cluster of instrument dials was instantly recognizable. But the move to digital cockpit displays put an end to that. Now, the new HMI paradigm from Munich is the Panoramic Vision display, which blends into the windscreen’s frit (the black border that’s painted on). The display is clear and quite minimalist but very legible, appearing a few inches further down the hood and thus closer to where your eyes focus on the road than if you had to look down at a conventional dash. It first showed up in the iX3 and now arrives in the bigger X5. While it looks unfamiliar at first—and people sure seem to hate the unfamiliar these days—together with the full-color heads-up display, you rarely need to look down into the cockpit while driving.

That goes for interacting with the infotainment system, too. The trapezoidal touchscreen and BMW’s current iDrive OS user interface are easy to use, but the onboard personal assistant works much better than the Alexa-based system did last year in the early iX3 we drove. I recognize that I’m an outlier using voice commands to interact with the car, but when they work, I’m going to use them. Particularly in the absence of physical controls—“Hey BMW, turn on the driver’s seat massager” is easier for me to do behind the wheel than tapping the car icon to access vehicle settings and then scrolling down to seats and then selecting the tab for massage and then turning it on.

There’s also a passenger screen, although, helpfully, BMW made this its own option rather than including it in a package. The screen only allows the front seat passenger to watch streaming videos, play games, or browse the web—they cannot interact with native infotainment functions like navigation or the climate settings from that screen, just the one to its left.

Another difference between the gasoline X5 and the iX5 is that the latter features BMW’s new “Heart of Joy.” This is one of the powerful domain controller computers that replaces the jumble of black boxes and single-function ECUs, in this case the one that manages vehicle dynamics. As we found with the iX3, this clever electronic brain enables solid chassis and powertrain control, including the ability to come to an incredibly smooth stop while one-pedal driving.

But the iX5 has another party trick that I didn’t notice in the smaller, cheaper EV: It will automatically detect red lights and stop signs, alerting you and braking the car if necessary (i.e., you were about to run the light or sign). The feature works whether you’ve engaged active drive assist or not. It’s always there like a safety net along with the car’s other advanced driver assistance systems. (I am sure you can disable this feature like the others, although I didn’t check, and I’m sure people will post comments with their particular edge case. Given driving standards these days, I’d be happier if everyone left it running.)

The new assist suite is called BMW Symbiotic Drive, and it’s of the very latest generation of ADAS that allows the driver to apply brake inputs without canceling out of active driving mode—only a heavy stomp on the brake will shut off cruise control.

Neither X5 nor iX5 are unpleasant to drive. The X5’s engine is quiet, and neither car suffers from much wind noise. Unlike the iX, which had something of a “skyhook” magic carpet ride, both iX5 and X5 are more firmly sprung, but not bone-rattlingly so. But I give the edge to the heavier iX5—although the battery adds to a hefty 6,200 lb (2,813 kg) curb weight, the extra mass helps dampen the short-duration shocks that make it past the X5’s (optional) adaptive air suspension. Longer-duration bumps are smoothed out by either car.

If you have passengers in the iX5, you might find Sport mode has too violent an initial throttle tip-in; in the other throttle settings (eco, comfort), this is not an issue. The iX5 also offers five levels of lift-off regenerative braking, from none at all (it coasts very well) to 0.6 G of regen. And it has true one-pedal driving that will bring you to a complete stop.

The 2027 X5 40 xDrive starts at $72,100, plus a $1,450 delivery and handling charge, and you can already find them in BMW showrooms. There is still a premium for the electric version—144 kWh of lithium-ion isn’t cheap, after all. Thus, the iX5 60 xDrive starts at $79,800 plus delivery and arrives in Q1 2027.

item.title: “Disillusioned” MAHA leader quits as Trump admin’s food agenda spoils: Report
item.description:
The departure comes amid turmoil in Kennedy’s Make America Healthy Again movement.

Calley Means—a top ally to anti-vaccine Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and a co-author of the so-called “MAHA bible”—resigned from his role in the Trump administration Thursday, reportedly in frustration over delays to food policy changes sought by the Make America Healthy Again movement.

“I am resigning from the White House with tremendous respect for President Trump and Bobby Kennedy,” Means wrote ina social media post this afternoon. “It was an honor to advocate for MAHA moms in the administration and steer policies like Dietary Guidelines reform, psychedelic reform, removing soda from SNAP, removing food dyes, GRAS reform, and overhauling government food procurement.”

His post did not provide a reason for his departure. Means served as a senior advisor to Kennedy.

Sources close to Means toldThe Wall Street Journalthat he had grown frustrated in the position. Means reportedly blamed other members of the administration for allowing the food industry and special interests to have too much sway in policy decisions. One source described Means as “disillusioned.”

The Journal recently reported that the White House had punted on two of Kennedy’s food priorities: defining and regulating ultraprocessed foods, and regulations that would require school meals to have more protein and less sugar. In recent meetings, Means reportedly raised his voice and grew visibly frustrated over the lack of progress on such issues. Others in the administration complained he was unwilling to make political concessions.

Means’ resignation comes as members of the MAHA movement have grown increasingly critical of Kennedy’s inability to follow through with key policy priorities. There is also growing backlash to Kennedy’s seeming embrace of corporate interests.A MAHA summit last monthdrew scorn for having numerous corporate sponsors, including Walmart, UnitedHealth, Anthropic, OpenAI, and Grail. Sponsorship packages were reportedly sold for up to $300,000. At the summit, Kennedy sat down for a “fireside chat” with Vice President JD Vance and extolled the potential of artificial intelligence. Many MAHA members and leaders felt betrayed by the corporate involvement, saying it was antithetical to the grassroots nature of the MAHA movement.

Means is among the early leaders of the grassroots effort. Along with his sister,Casey Means, he co-authored a book considered the “MAHA bible,” titledGood Energy: The Surprising Connection Between Metabolism and Limitless Health. The book provides a potpourri of dietary and lifestyle advice, including recommendations to avoid processed foods, seed oils, fragrances, various home care products, fluoride, unfiltered water, bananas (when eaten alone), receipt paper, and birth control pills. One of its chapters is titled “Trust Yourself, Not Your Doctor.”

Trump nominated Casey Means to be surgeon general, buther nomination was abandonedamid misgivings over her medical qualifications, positions on vaccines, and promotion of unproven wellness claims.

item.title: Ink droplets in motion snag top prize in Nikon Small World contest
item.description:
Ole Bielfeldt of Germany captured a microscopic view of an inkjet printer depositing ink onto paper.

A 25-year-old German experimental photographer has won the 2026 Nikon Small World photomicrography competition with a striking image of droplets of ink being deposited on paper by an inkjet printer. Ole Bielfeldt beat out 1,802 other entries hailing from 69 different countries.

Bielfeldt became interested in photomicrography during the COVID-19 lockdown after discovering an old microscope in his parents’ attic. He figured out how to build an adaptor out of a tube and some wood to connect the microscope to his father’s camera and taught himself the art through trial and error, building custom tools as needed. Hedocumentshow he captures transformative images of everyday objects with behind-the-scenes videos posted tomacrofying, his photography and videography brand.

It was Bielfeldt’s curiosity about the inner workings of inkjet printers that inspired his winning entry, but capturing the action of ink drops being deposited on paper was a challenge, given that the process happens so quickly. The droplets, for instance, moved faster than the camera’s shutter speed. Bielfeldt’s solution was to deconstruct the printer so that the paper moved under a stationary (rather than moving) printhead, and then take the image in a dark room, using a flash to serve as the shutter, thereby freezing the ink drops mid-air. There was no need for pricey equipment. Bielfeldt does not use AI in his images, preferring to rely on traditional techniques.

“Ole Bielfeldt’s winning image embodies what makes Nikon Small World so powerful: the intersection of microscope imaging, ingenuity, and artistry,”said Eric Flem, a spokesperson for Nikon Instruments. “By using a microscope objective in a different way, he transformed a familiar object into something altogether new and previously unseen. It is a reminder that the microscope is not only a scientific tool but also a creative one, capable of expanding how we see and imagine the world around us.”

Founded in 1974, the Nikon Small World competition celebrates its 52nd anniversary this year. In 2011, the company added the Small World in Motion competition (see the2026 winner here). Both are meant “to showcase the beauty and complexity of things seen through the light microscope”—one through still photographs, the other through photovideography, taking advantage of all the technological advances that now allow users to make movies or time-lapse images through the microscope.

Here are the top 10 winners of this year’s competition; the full list, with honorable mentions, can be foundhere. Nikon is also producing a full-color 2027 calendar featuring the 2026 winners.

item.title: Leaked Mass Effect: Universe trailer gives a taste of what we’re all missing
item.description:
We can’t have nice things, but at least we can get trailers for them.

Those mourning yesterday’sshuttering of highly praised and influential developer BioWarealso had to deal with the cancellation of the nextMass Effectgame, which wasfirst teased back in 2020. Today, we got our best look at what that game could have been with a short, leaked trailer forMass Effect: Universe.

In the roughly two-minute montage—which describes itself as “in-engine footage from our small team” that “uses our pre-production assets”—an ex-military officer wearing an N7 trenchcoat (similar to the one seen in that 2020 teaser) encounters an Asari at a bar. He talks of his frustration with military life—“by the time you put out one fire, another had already started”—before discussing his new line of work “stopping [the fires] before they start” and “making the choices no one else is willing to make. Going where others are afraid to go.”

As the intriguing Asari at the bar reveals herself to be the one who metaphorically “start[s] the fires,” N7 allies reveal themselves as backup. The cutscene transitions seamlessly into an all-out group gunfight in the bar, complete with hostiles being stuck in place inside mass effect fields and others being crushed by furniture brought down on top of them.

The action-packed bar scene is interspersed with short vignettes from around the game’s universe, including a hovercraft speeding over an icy planet, an examination of a truly gigantic alien suspended in a glass cylinder, and a team looking at a holographic map dotted with dozens of points of interest.

The existence of the internalMass Effect: Universetrailer was firstrevealed by an anonymous Reddit poster yesterdayand thenconfirmed by IGNearly Thursday morning. The trailer videoappeared on Redditslightly before noon Eastern time, with mods there saying they couldn’t “independently verify the authenticity” but that it “seems legitimate.” Within hours, bothIGNandBloomberg’s Jason Schreierhad confirmed that the trailer was authentic and came from someone inside EA.

Following yesterday’s BioWare closure announcement, sci-fi authors Catherynne M. Valente and Derek Kunskenbothrevealedthey had been working on the game for years. “It was one of the greatest privileges & GLORIOUS challenges of my life. I smiled every day. I worked HARD for the fans, every day,” Valente wrote. “What we were cooking was really cool,” Kunsken added.

Despite the existence of a 6-year-old teaser for the game, EA executives Cam Weber and David Tinson said in a memo to staff yesterday that there was only “a small team at BioWare working on early-development forMass Effect.” The decision “not to move forward with this development” led to BioWare’s closure, which the note calls “a legendary studio that helped define the role-playing genre, and we do not take this decision lightly.”

Inan N7 Day blog post last year, Executive Producer Mike Gamble said, “The team is heads-down and focused exclusively onMass Effect. We have a lot of universe to cover, lots of features to build, and lots of romances to figure out. We’re excited by what we’re building, and we promise you: when we’re ready, it’ll be a lot of fun to show.”

“Your support has meant everything to me over the past 17 years at BioWare,” Gamblewrote yesterday on social media.

Despite the game’s cancellation, the Mass Effect universe will still be represented on streaming TV screens.IGNcites “sources inside Prime Video” in reporting that the streaming seriesfirst announced in 2024is still in active development.

As for the series’s future in gaming, anInternet petitionhas predictably popped up urging EA to continue funding development of the series or license the IP to an outside studio. The petition has nearly 17,500 signatories as of this writing, though thosepetitioners face an uphill battleconvincingEA’s new private ownershipto focus on a massive narrative action RPG and notmore profitable franchiseslikeBattlefield,The Sims, and annual sports releases.

item.title: Disgraced eMudhra drops out of TLS business after using cert private key of 4
item.description:
Flubbed key signing “ceremony” allowed minting of web credentials for any site.

eMudra, the certificate authority that issued eight intermediate TLS credentials so weak that anyone could mint certificates for any website or mail server—one had a private encryption key of just 4—said it’s getting out of the business.

V. Srinivasan, chairman of India-based eMudhra Limited,citedincreasing costs and complexities of compliance requirements—paired with the business generating just 1 percent of its revenue. He also said that the emergence of organizations providing TLS certificates free of charge further reduced returns on investment when compared to other products and services the company offers.

“However, the level of social media amplification around this incident has brought scrutiny that is out of proportion to SSL/TLS’s place in our business,” the company continued in a Thursday post. “In view of this, after detailed deliberations our board has concluded that withdrawing from global SSL/TLS is the right decision for eMudhra and its shareholders.”

The announcement came two days after researchers revealed eMudhra had issued eight certificates with private keys so defective theyweretrivial to discover. Anyone who took the time—which wasmeasured in milliseconds—could crack them and then use them to generate TLS certificates that would be trusted by all major browsers, as well as an untold number of email servers, IoT devices, Docker containers, forgotten Linux machines, and unmaintained CLI tools that ship their own copy of the roots.

Whereas NIST P-384 elliptic curve cryptography private keys—used in the type of certificates eMudhra issued—are supposed to contain roughly 384 bits of entropy, the eight compromised certificates had key sizes ranging from 3 to 8 bits. Stated differently, whereas there are supposed to be 2384—a number with 116 digits—different key possibilities, the strongest of the defective keys had a maximum of just 256. The private keys were 4, 56, 66, 115, 155, 156, 230, 237.

Browser makers blocked certificates that were issued with the intermediate certificates within a day or two of them being discovered. eMudhra almost certainly faced the prospect of its certificate authority status being pulled by the CA/Browser Forum, an industry-wide group that sets rules for admittance into the TLS certificate program.

On Wednesday, eMudhra provided a brief explanation for the debacle. The certificates were “created under eMudhra’s ECC root in a Key Generation Ceremony (KGC) held on April 30, 2025, using FIPS 140-2 Level 3 Hardware Security Modules (HSMs),” the companysaid. “A flaw in the KGC caused a wrap/unwrap step to produce a second set of weak keys alongside the original strong keys. The weak keys were the ones published to the browser root stores. eMudhra is working to establish the root cause.”

HSMs are dedicated devices for storing encryption keys and other highly sensitive data. They are generally segregated from most of a network to prevent leakage. Wrapping and unwrapping refers to the process that occurs when keys are being transferred from one HSM to another. Before the handover, the HSM storing the key wraps it in a separate key. Once the encrypted key is moved to a new HSM, the latter unwraps the key.

In a thread on Mozilla’s Bugzilla forum, eMudhra providedmore details: Among them:

[T]here appears to be a flaw in the KGC script that was used on that specific day to create these ECC issuers. As for these ECC keys, our review of the KGC, assessment of the code and view of HSM keys so far indicate that a) a set of original ECC keys were created onboard as expected b) an approved deviation to our usual KGC to test a wrap/unwrap was introduced as these keys were meant for export for this instance c) a flaw in the code resulted in the second pair of keys being created onboard which were weaker d) these second pair of weaker keys were used by mistake to create the csr [certificate signing request] (because the key labels were similar) and signed by our root e) the CSR from these weaker keys were also sent over to [fellow certificate authority] Sectigo for cross signing (we verified the files sent over to Sectigo).

Additionally, eMudhra said:

The CRL’s were signed with the original private keys (which were supposed to be the correct keys with appropriate entropy) but given that this resulted in incorrect signatures, they were resigned with flawed keys.

There were human errors in multiple steps of the process that resulted in significant flaws in the key lifecycle integrity process for this KGC. We are now digging deeper for code flaws, process gaps, maker/checker controls specific to this issue. Over the next week, we will reverify every key ceremony we have done.

A CRL, short for certificate revocation list, is a digitally signed list published by a certificate authority identifying certificates that have been revoked before their expiration dates. The revelation that the initial signing resulted in incorrect CRL signatures raises the question: why didn’t eMudhra investigate the cause of the failure?

With the intermediate certificates blocked by browsers, much of the threat is gone. But plenty of other devices that rely on the same certificates require much longer windows to take the same action. Still other devices, such as embedded devices, may never be able to block them.

]]>

item.title: Comcast loses more customers, claims other ISPs’ cheap prices are “irrational”
item.description:
Comcast plans job cuts and more AI agents for its shrinking cable customer base.

Comcast reportedly plans significant job cuts in its cable division as the firm continues to lose residential broadband and TV customers. Comcast lost 144,000 residential broadband customers in Q3 2026, up from a 91,000-customer loss in the same quarter a year ago, the company said in itsearnings reporttoday.

Comcast historically capitalized on a lack of competition for high-speed wired broadband. But now it faces stronger competition from fixed wireless providers and from fiber providers in parts of its cable territory.

“Fixed wireless remains aggressive and continues to take share, while fiber construction remains elevated, with pockets of irrational pricing and promotional activity,” Comcast co-CEO Mike Cavanagh said today in anearnings call.

Comcast CFO Jason Armstrong said “irrational pricing” from fiber operators includes $30 to $40 monthly broadband offers “in specific markets in the third quarter.” He said $30 to $40 pricing is irrational because deploying fiber costs $1,500 or more per home, and is “getting more expensive with construction costs up as you get into more suburban and rural areas.”

“As we look at the return profile of that, to us, that is irrational competition,” Armstrong said. While he didn’t name any specific competitors, Verizon has been pitching FiOS fiber plans that start at $30 a month. Comcast’s network is a mix of fiber and cable, and it offers fiber-to-the-home in onlysmall portionsof its cable territory.

Armstrong said more Comcast customers are leaving when they face “pricing transitions,” apparently referring to the price hikes customers get when promotional offers expire. “We’ve been refining our offers and retention strategies to better manage these transitions and strengthen customer retention,” he said.

Cavanagh said that “satellite is not yet a material factor” in the competition Comcast faces, but that Comcast is focused on “anticipating emerging forms of competition and positioning our business to respond as the market evolves.”

After the latest quarterly drop, Comcast has 28.3 million residential broadband customers in the US. Comcast said it has a plan to turn things around.

“We’ve embarked on the most significant operating and cost transformation in our company’s history, with an opportunity we believe will ultimately amount to billions of dollars over time,” Cavanagh said. The organizational changes will result in a “significant charge” of over $1 billion to be applied in the fourth quarter earnings report, Armstrong said.

It appears likely that job cuts will affect Comcast’s famously frustrating customer service division, replacing some number of humans with AI agents that already handle some customer interactions. “As personal AI agents reshape how consumers discover, purchase, and manage services, we’re positioning Comcast to capitalize on that shift,” Armstrong said.

As is typically the case when companies announce layoffs, Comcast said the goal is not merely reducing salary. Cavanagh said Comcast’s plan “goes well beyond cost savings” and will “create a more agile, efficient organization that can compete more effectively and invest more decisively in growth.”

Comcast lost 274,000 video customers in the quarter, up from a 257,000-customer loss in the same quarter last year. Total video customers are down to 10.4 million. Comcast added 368,000 wireless lines, down from a 414,000-line gain last year. It now has 10.6 million wireless lines in its business of offering mobile service to broadband subscribers.

Bloombergreported yesterdaythat “Comcast is planning a significant number of job cuts as part of an overall restructuring of its cable-TV, broadband and wireless businesses.” AVariety reporttoday said the number of job cuts isn’t yet determined, but that “the layoffs are expected to affect the Comcast Cable side of the business, not NBCU divisions,” referring to Comcast’s NBCUniversal subsidiary. Comcast did not provide any specifics on job-cut plans when contacted by Ars today.

Comcast also plans to split itself into two publicly traded companies through a spinoff of NBCUniversal and Sky. The spinoff planwas announced in Juneand is expected to be completed in mid-2027. Comcast’s company-wide revenue was $29.3 billion in the third quarter, down from $31.2 billion the previous year. Net income rose from $3.33 billion to $3.45 billion.

Comcast’s stock price increased today afterbeating analyst expectationsfor its overall earnings, which included a profit from its Peacock streaming service. But it lost more broadband customers than expected and gained fewer wireless lines than expected.

“Comcast’s connectivity-and-platforms revenue fell 2.6 percent in constant currency in the third quarter, to $19.66 billion,” The Wall Street Journalwrote. “That was a steeper loss than what Wall Street had expected. The company also added fewer domestic wireless lines than it did a year earlier, missing analyst estimates.”

Comcast’s total broadband subscribers rose every quarter for 20 years until itreported a net lossof 10,000 residential broadband customers in Q2 2022. In Q1 2025, a net loss of 183,000 residential broadband customers caused Cavanagh to bemoan that the company isn’t “winning in the marketplace.”

Comcast tried to turn things around byproviding unlimited dataon plans that previously had monthly data caps and by offering a five-year price guarantee. Its five-year price guarantee plans start at $45 a month before taxes and fees. Customer lossescontinued despite those changes.

Comcast provides free wireless lines for a year to its broadband customers, but said this is not an irrational offer. “When we offer a free wireless line, it is against zero capital deployed,” Armstrong said, noting that Comcast resells mobile capacity instead of building its own cellular network. “We don’t have spectrum. We don’t have towers. Our model is an MVNO [Mobile Virtual Network Operator] model.”

Obtaining mobile capacity through Comcast’s MVNO agreement with Verizon isn’t free, of course. But Armstrong said Comcast customers who receive a free wireless line for a year “are converting into paying subscribers within a year to a very rational price point, we think, and our goal is obviously to upsell them over time.”

The price of a basic Comcast mobile line goes from free to $30 a month after one year, and requires a bundle with Comcast home Internet. Armstrong said Comcast is “converting 70 percent of those free lines into paying relationships.”

Armstrong also discussed Comcast’s plan to increase use of AI agents to interact with customers. It’s up to customers to determine whether this improves service or makes things worse, but it will apparently be cheaper for Comcast.

“AI is already embedded across our network to optimize performance, and we’re expanding its application across customer experience through partnerships with Sierra and Cresta,” Armstrong said. “These capabilities are central to our new operating model, enabling us to bring products to market faster, simplifying customer interactions, and deliver a better experience more efficiently. We’ve already reduced customer service contact rates by roughly 20 percent and eliminated more than 30 million service interactions year-to-date versus the prior year.”

item.title: Latest estimate for Starship launches required to support a Moon landing? 22.
item.description:
“We need to keep our eyes on numerous required fuelings for the lander.”

NASA does not have, nor want, nuclear weapons. But when it comes to a particular metric that is part of the Artemis Program to land people on the Moon, NASA guards a particular number like they are trying to prevent outsiders from cracking nuclear codes.

I am speaking of the number of Starship launches required to fuel a Starship-based lunar lander in low-Earth orbit such that it can fly out to the Moon, land there, and return to lunar orbit.

This number has been a moving target over the years. The general response from NASA has typically been, ‘We don’t know for sure, so we’re not going to say.’ In 2023, for example, the then-director of NASA’s Human Landing System, Lisa Watson-Morgan,told Ars, “We have a general idea, but I’m reluctant to say exactly what that is.”

Later, she said the number was in the “high single digits to the low double digits.” That suggests about a dozen launches, which is a lot. SpaceX would need to launch a “depot” Starship, and then 11 “tanker” Starships to fully load it with liquid oxygen and methane propellant for a lunar voyage. Other officials have said “high teens.” The hope has always been that SpaceX would dramatically improve the lift capacity of Starship to bring down the number of tanker flights.

But now there are concerns among some NASA officials that this might not be happening, or at least not happening soon enough to allow SpaceX’s Starship rocket to play a meaningful role in returning humans to the Moon for NASA as part of Artemis this decade.

On Thursday, the NASA Aerospace Safety Advisory Panel held its quarterly meeting, during which panel member Charlie Precourt (a former NASA astronaut) spoke about risks associated with the Artemis Program and landing humans on the Moon.

“With respect to Artemis IV, however, we’ve got a large number of firsts that reduce the likelihood of mission success,” Precourt said. “We need to keep our eyes on numerous required fuelings for the lander. I think the last estimate is around 22 flights.”

Precourt did not name Starship, but he could only be referring to the SpaceX vehicle. NASA’s other lunar lander for human missions, Blue Origin’s Blue Moon, will not be using orbital refueling as part of its initial mission design. The safety panel almost certainly would have obtained this estimated number of refuelings, 22, from discussions with NASA officials as part of its deliberations during quarterly meetings.

After I posted Precourt’s estimate on the social media site X, SpaceX founder Elon Musk replied that NASA’s safety panel estimate was not accurate. “That’s way too high,”Musk said. “Actual number will be more like 6 to 8.”

To be fair to NASA and SpaceX, there remains a lot of uncertainty in how much cryogenic methane and liquid oxygen will boil off in orbit and how efficient the process of transferring propellants from one ship to another will be. But NASA can take the current performance of the lift capacity of Starship and determine the mass of propellant needed to support a lunar landing. For now, the space agency’s answer to the Starship question appears to be something on the order of two dozen Starship launches.

SpaceX, of course,is working hardto increase the flight rate of Starship. But even if SpaceX achieves “twice weekly” launches by the end of 2027, the company would still need about three months to fuel a depot for a Starship landing.

Precourt said the problem is a challenging one for NASA, and he praised the space agency chief, Jared Isaacman, and his team for trying to find ways to help SpaceX and Blue Origin be successful in their development of landers. NASA is still working toward a human lunar landing in 2028.

“With respect to schedule, I personally really appreciate the focus the administrator and the leadership team is putting on how to press schedule by bringing in resources to enable it to look for places where there are barriers,” he said.
